extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent prosecutors, in-house counsel, and judges evaluating §101 patent-eligibility
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and compiled case holdings used to evaluate whether patent claims are directed to an abstract idea and whether they contain an 'inventive concept' under Alice/Mayo. The page lists examples and courts' reasoning across technologies to illustrate eligibility/ineligibility outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed to an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claims are 'directed to' an abstract idea (e.g., collecting, organizing, analyzing, and presenting data; account management; transmitting routine business communications; vote collection and verification; message routing; providing customized directions; selecting a receiver connection based on encoding format).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page repeatedly lists holdings where courts found claims directed to abstract ideas, using many concrete examples: 'collecting and organizing information about available real estate properties and displaying this information on a digital map'; 'using notebook-type tabs to label and organize spreadsheets'; 'collecting, storing, and sharing information of registered users'; 'tailoring marketing communications to recipients'; 'receipt, processing, and display of data'; 'providing advertisement inserts with newspapers.' These examples indicate that routine data manipulation, conventional business practices, and longstanding human activities implemented on computers are often characterized as abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of inventive concept — generic computer components
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims lack an 'inventive concept' when they 'require only generic computer components' or merely implement the abstract idea on a generic computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple holdings state that reciting generic hardware or conventional computer technology is insufficient to supply an inventive concept (e.g., claims that 'recited only generic hardware', 'provided no improvement over the existing art', or 'recited generic computer components functioning in a conventional manner').

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must recite specific ways, hardware, or software (not just functions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility favors claims that recite specific ways to perform the invention, particular hardware, or software-based implementation details rather than high-level functional results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts denied eligibility where the claims 'did not recite any “specific ways, hardware or software,” to carry out the claims' or 'failed to recite a means of achieving that result.' The absence of concrete implementation details tends to support a finding of abstraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement to computer/technology required for eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are more likely eligible if they provide a specific improvement to computer functionality or to a technological process, rather than merely using computers as a tool to perform an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples on the page: claims that used 'engine frequency to measure run time' were considered 'innovative technology'; the tangible resumption of an interrupted file download was held to represent a 'specific improvement to a computer's capabilities'; claims improving data transmission over wireless networks were not abstract. Courts look for a specific, concrete contribution to the technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the problem is 'rooted in computer technology'
rubrics_metrics.description: If the problem the claim purports to solve is not 'necessarily rooted in computer technology,' courts may treat the claim as abstract and ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A holding noted ineligibility because the 'purportedly solved problem was not one “necessarily rooted in computer technology”.' Thus, showing that the claimed invention addresses a technical problem specific to computers supports eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims implementing conventional/longstanding business practices are abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementing a longstanding business practice, human activity, or conventional business process on a computer is treated as an abstract idea absent additional inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page holdings include many business/practice examples: 'account management', 'using a third-party intermediary to connect services', 'establishing a cross-reference resource', 'tailoring marketing communications', 'transmitting compressed images to facilitate buying/selling.' Courts repeatedly found such claims ineligible when they simply automated conventional practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical algorithms and data-processing methods are often abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are essentially mathematical methodologies (e.g., converting geospatial coordinates to numbers, predictive analytics, generating a histogram) are treated as abstract ideas unless tied to a technological improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases cited include mathematical conversions, predictive analytics, and histogram generation. Courts held these claims ineligible where they were just algorithms or computations with no inventive technological application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must recite new or improved physical components to show patentable invention
rubrics_metrics.description: When claims involve physical devices (RFID readers, transponders, antennas, videophones, etc.), eligibility favors claims that describe a new or improved physical component; absence of such improvements weighed against eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes holdings that claims failed because they did not 'describe a new or improved RFID transponder, a new or improved RFID reader, or a new or improved RFID antenna,' and where the specification did not disclose an improved videophone.

rubrics_metrics.name: No presumption of eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are not automatically presumed eligible; courts may explicitly hold that claims 'are not entitled to a presumption of eligibility.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At least one holding explicitly states that claims are not entitled to a presumption of eligibility, signaling that courts apply the Alice framework without an initial presumption in favor of eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to show improvement over the prior art undermines eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that do not demonstrate an improvement over existing technology or the prior art are likely to lack an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several entries note ineligibility because the claims 'provided no improvement over the existing art' or there was 'no evidence that the claims improved computer functionality.' Demonstrating improvement over prior art is a common route to show inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim limitations must correspond to physical or functional aspects of the described system
rubrics_metrics.description: When claim limitations do not 'correspond to any physical or functional aspect of the described system,' courts have found no inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A cited holding said the limitations did not 'correspond to any physical or functional aspect of the described system,' which supported ineligibility. Claims should tie limitations to tangible system aspects where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic Internet implementations that do not override routine sequences are ineligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that merely implement abstract ideas over the Internet using routine sequences of events, without changing how the Internet or its protocols operate, are ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: claims were held lacking inventive concept because they 'did not override any routine sequence of events on the Internet.' Courts examine whether the claim changes the conventional online behavior or merely automates it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine data collection/analysis/display is abstract absent a technical solution
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are limited to collecting, organizing, analyzing, and displaying data are treated as abstract unless they recite a specific technical means or improvement for performing those tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many case holdings found ineligibility for claims described as 'collecting, organizing, comparing, and presenting data,' 'collecting information, analyzing it, and displaying results,' or 'collecting and reporting the missing power of a network device' when no specific technological contribution was present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific, concrete contribution to the technology is required
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts look for a 'specific, concrete contribution to the technology' (e.g., tangible improvements, specialized hardware/software) as evidence of eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A number of holdings reversed ineligibility when claims were found to involve 'a specific means of achieving' a technological goal or a 'specific improvement to a computer’s capabilities.' The guidance from cases is to craft claims and specifications that identify concrete technical advances.
